common_name: St. Cecilia Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring or fall; St. Cecilia was one of David Austin's earlier English roses, introduced in 1987, combining old-rose cupped form and myrrh fragrance with repeat bloom, and performs through Gulf South heat with better disease resistance than many roses of its class.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2.5-3.5 feet apart. Introduced by David Austin in 1987, St. Cecilia was among his earlier English roses and remains a favorite for its soft, blush-apricot, cupped, old-fashioned-looking blooms and strong myrrh fragrance, an unusual scent profile distinct from the classic damask or tea fragrances of most roses. The relatively lax, arching shrub blooms in flushes from late spring through fall and shows better disease resistance than many early English roses, though like most of the class it benefits from good air circulation and occasional attention to blackspot in humid climates. It works well in mixed borders and cottage-style plantings, where its graceful, informal habit and soft coloring blend easily with perennials. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage a compact shape and vigorous new flowering growth.

common_name: Gruss an Aachen Rose (Antique Peachy-Pink Floribunda)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Gruss an Aachen is an 1909 German rose often considered the first floribunda, valued for large, old-fashioned, peachy-pink-to-cream blooms and compact, disease-resistant growth well suited to the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in Germany in 1909, Gruss an Aachen ('greetings from Aachen') is historically significant as one of the roses credited with founding the floribunda class, produced by crossing a hybrid tea with a polyantha to combine large, full-form blooms with the polyantha's compact habit and cluster-flowering vigor. Its large, fully double, old-fashioned-shaped blooms open warm peachy-pink and fade to soft cream, with a moderate, pleasant fragrance, on a low, bushy, well-branched shrub that blooms in generous, repeated flushes from spring through fall. It shows good resistance to blackspot for an early-20th-century rose and needs little care beyond routine watering and an annual light shaping. The compact size makes it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and maintain a tidy shape.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Gruss an Aachen variety notes

common_name: Cramoisi Supérieur Rose (Crimson Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Cramoisi Supérieur is an 1832 French China rose valued for deep crimson-red blooms and the class's characteristic heat and humidity tolerance, making it a long-standing favorite in Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1832, Cramoisi Supérieur ('superior crimson') bears cupped, fully double, rich crimson-red blooms with a light fragrance, borne in small clusters against dark green, glossy foliage typical of the China rose class. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through the first hard frost and shares the exceptional heat, humidity, and disease tolerance for which China roses are prized in the Gulf South, needing little to no spraying to stay healthy through the growing season. A climbing sport of the variety is also grown, but the shrub form remains the most widely planted, working well in borders, mass plantings, and as a low, informal hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; heavy pruning is unnecessary since flowering continues on both old and new growth.

common_name: Sombreuil Rose (Antique White Climbing Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a support; Sombreuil is an 1850 climbing tea rose prized for flat, quartered, creamy-white blooms and strong performance in the heat and humidity of Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor, allowing 4-6 feet for its climbing spread. Introduced in France in 1850, Sombreuil is a climbing tea rose bearing large, flat, densely quartered, creamy-white blooms tinged with the faintest blush of pink, carrying a light tea fragrance and considered one of the finest white antique climbers for its old-fashioned flower form. It blooms repeatedly from spring through fall, most heavily in spring, and performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with good resistance to blackspot compared to many climbing roses. Train the long canes horizontally along a fence or arbor rather than straight up a post, since horizontally trained canes produce far more flowering side-shoots than vertical ones. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to remove spent wood, saving any structural pruning for full winter dormancy.

common_name: Buff Beauty Rose (Apricot-Buff Hybrid Musk Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Buff Beauty is a 1939 English hybrid musk rose valued for warm apricot-buff clustered blooms, strong fragrance, and better tolerance of part shade than most roses.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart to allow for its broad, spreading habit. Bred by Ann Bentall and introduced in England in 1939, Buff Beauty is a hybrid musk rose bearing large clusters of warm apricot-buff, fully double blooms with a strong, sweet musk fragrance, aging to a soft cream as they open. As a hybrid musk, it is more shade-tolerant than most roses, flowering respectably with as little as four to five hours of direct sun, which makes it useful in gardens where a fully open, all-day-sun spot isn't available. The lax, arching canes can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence, and the plant blooms in flushes from late spring through fall with good resistance to blackspot. Prune back by about a third in late winter if grown as a shrub, or simply thin out old wood if trained as a climber, since Buff Beauty flowers on both old and new growth.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Buff Beauty variety notes
American Rose Society — Hybrid Musk Rose Class Descriptions
